title: United States–Japan Strategic Energy & Industrial Partnership
subtitle: Where deeper industrial integration creates strategic value, through which instruments, and where to stay out
label: Generated from Allied Industrial Base Explorer data and a curated external evidence layer (accessed 2026-11-06); evidence, sources and caveats in the appendix. Data as of 30 October 2026.
disclosure: Rule-generated from the data (R/partnerships) with external facts from a dated, curated evidence layer; not yet checked by an independent verifier. Items marked partial or unverified must be confirmed before citation.

inlines.v: Permanent Magnets & Drive Systems: Rare-earth oxides & compounds (joint); Rare-earth permanent magnets (Japan->US). Battery Materials & Cells: Natural graphite (joint); Accumulator parts & separators (Japan->US). Solar Manufacturing: Polysilicon (US->Japan). Wind & Hydropower Equipment: Wind turbine generating sets (US->Japan).

Recognise trusted partner supply of electric vehicles extraction (cobalt ores, lithium minerals, natural graphite); wind turbine generating sets; accumulator parts & separators in procurement and content rules. Common anti-circumvention rules for electric vehicles refining (rare-earth metals, rare-earth oxides & compounds) and rare-earth oxides & compounds. Keep uranium/fuel extraction: aggregated low-coverage sub-sectors (spent fuel & nuclear scrap, uranium ores); pgms (iridium, ruthenium); nuclear special materials open to global sourcing.
Upgrade Japan-US Strategic Investment Initiative (MOU of 4 Sep 2025): sector strategy, reciprocal commitments, a KPI dashboard and an annual review. No new MOU.
Do not co-subsidise new Automatic controllers capacity. Do not co-subsidise new Gas components capacity. Do not co-subsidise new Semiconductor manufacturing equipment capacity.

Of 142 technology x stage cells and electro-industrial nodes assessed for the pair, 35 show an active complementarity (a supplier meeting the other's need, a shared chokepoint, a capacity-constrained trusted supplier or a chain specialisation), 4 direct competition and 79 no strategic case. The relationship is not one of general similarity: most of the electro-industrial base needs no bilateral intervention.

AIB strategic roles: US Demand & Market Anchor (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (primary), Capital & Investment Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (secondary), Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (secondary); Japan Capital & Investment Anchor (primary), Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (secondary).

Japan supplies specialised processed materials and components where the US is short (accumulator parts & separators, rare-earth permanent magnets, wafers, battery materials (foil, electrolyte)); the US supplies polysilicon, wind turbine generating sets, battery recycling feed where Japan is short; and the two share exposure to the same coercive supplier in rare-earth oxides & compounds and natural graphite, where neither can supply the other and the answer is joint demand, finance and third-country capacity.

The US brings demand, offtake and capital to Japan's capability; Japan brings specialised capacity and patient finance (JBIC, NEXI, JOGMEC) to the US's market. That is the trade: market access and demand certainty for trusted capacity.

Existing mechanisms and the MEA question
. Gaps: no cross-sector KPI dashboard or review cycle; no bilateral mechanism covers SC-SOLAR, SC-GRID; USJ-SII has a pipeline and finance but no reciprocal commitments or sector strategy.
Do not sign a new energy MOU. Give USJ-SII a sector strategy, reciprocal commitments and a KPI dashboard covering the recommended compacts, reviewed every 12 months.

This section sets out what already exists before anything new is proposed. Facts are from the curated evidence layer (accessed 2026-11-06); items marked partial or unverified rest on secondary sources and should be confirmed before citation.
Japan's memberships in OSI's economic-security agreements table: G7, IPEF, MSP.

Quad foreign ministers adopted a framework to mobilise up to $20bn for secure critical-mineral supply chains; a separate July 2025 Quad initiative is mentioned only in passing and not sourced.

Signed 28 Mar 2023 and in force on signature without congressional approval; covers cobalt/graphite/lithium/manganese/nickel; no export duties; consult on non-market measures and forced-labour imports; Treasury/USTR treated it as an FTA for the IRA EV credit critical-minerals test.

Japan government text states that for any Section 232 tariff on pharmaceuticals and semiconductors (incl. SME) the US intends to apply to Japan a rate no greater than that applied to any other country; search snippet only, full document not read.
EO signed 4 Sep 2025 sets 15% all-in tariff on Japanese goods (reciprocal) and a Section 232 auto/auto-parts rate that tops MFN up to 15% (added rate zero at or above 15%).
CRS (Apr 2026) describes the DTA as an executive agreement enacted without changes to US law.

IRS says the new clean vehicle credit (30D) is not allowed for vehicles acquired after 30 Sep 2025, so the CMA's IRA-credit eligibility function is largely moot; no source found on any formal CMA amendment or termination (status in force but unreviewed).

In Feb 2026 Akazawa said the sides were far apart on first projects; Lutnick claimed Trump has complete discretion while Akazawa said selection follows the investment and consultation committees; resolved only by the 17 Feb announcement; later disputes not found.

On 20 Feb 2026 the Court ruled 6-3 that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, removing the legal basis of the 15% Japan reciprocal rate; a temporary Section 122 global surcharge replaced it; Section 232 duties (autos etc.) unaffected.

Axios (30 Jun 2026) says Nippon reaffirmed an $11bn investment pledge with allocation of $7.8bn unspecified and mostly still promised, the golden share has not been used on management decisions, and leverage rose with an S&P downgrade; the deal closed 18 Jun 2025.

Jiji reports the US imposed new 12.5% Section 301 tariffs on Japan and dozens of partners after the Section 122 surcharge expired 24 Jul 2026; Japan called it regrettable and the 15% auto rate is said to be maintained; a separate excess-capacity 301 probe (launched Mar 2026) includes Japan. Check USTR Federal Register notice for final rate.
As of Sep 2026 Akazawa declined detail on a third tranche, with AI and semiconductor projects reported as leading candidates and no date; no third announcement found by 6 Nov 2026.

MOU signed 4 Sep 2025 (Lutnick/Akazawa): presidential investment committee chaired by Commerce Secretary consults a joint consultation committee; US proposes projects; Japan has 45 days to fund each approved project or may decline and forfeit distributions (President may raise tariffs); per-project SPVs split cash 50/50 then 90/10 to the US after a deemed allocation amount; investments before 19 Jan 2029; US Investment Accelerator executes.

Framework text dated 27 Oct 2025 (signed Tokyo 28 Oct) commits to financing within six months for selected projects (grants/guarantees/loans/equity/offtake/insurance), a ministerial within 180 days, faster permitting, pricing measures to support non-China supply, scrap recycling, a complementary stockpile arrangement, and a Rapid Response Group led by the US Energy Secretary and METI Minister; names no dollar amounts and is non-binding.
Framework establishes a group led by the US Energy Secretary and Japan's METI Minister to identify priority minerals and accelerate processed-mineral deliveries.

Greer announced the Action Plan on 19 Mar 2026: the two countries will develop strategic trade policies and border mechanisms to protect downstream industries and lay the foundation for a binding plurilateral agreement supported by price floors; trade press adds deep-sea R&D (not read from primary).

Signed 28 Mar 2023 and in force on signature without congressional approval; covers cobalt/graphite/lithium/manganese/nickel; no export duties; consult on non-market measures and forced-labour imports; Treasury/USTR treated it as an FTA for the IRA EV credit critical-minerals test.

Announced 28 Oct 2025 as preliminary pledges in a launch phase needing review; AA lists nuclear up to $332bn, Mitsubishi Electric AI infrastructure $30bn and Panasonic energy storage $15bn.
The fact sheet lists up to $100B for Westinghouse AP1000/SMR with possible Japanese supplier involvement (MHI Toshiba IHI); CSIS cites a separate figure of $80B in a US-Westinghouse partnership.
The fact sheet lists up to $100B for GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 SMR construction with Hitachi GE Vernova as a possible Japanese participant.
JERA (Sep 2025) and Tokyo Gas (6 Nov 2025) each signed non-binding LOIs for 1 MTPA from Alaska LNG; no binding SPA, JBIC financing or FID found, and it is not among announced SII projects.
One of the first three funded projects under the $550B vehicle is a $33B 9.2GW SB Energy gas plant in Portsmouth Ohio.

Commerce lists industrial synthetic diamond manufacturing at about $0.6bn in the first batch announced 17 Feb 2026; the Georgia site and Element Six (De Beers) operator come from secondary reporting only.
Commerce lists US crude oil export infrastructure at about $2.1bn in the first batch (17 Feb 2026); Sentinel Midstream's Texas GulfLink identification comes from secondary reporting only.
Commerce lists natural gas generation at about $33.3bn (first batch total about $36bn); the Ohio location and 9.2 GW size come from the Lutnick statement as quoted in secondary coverage.
ANS (17 Mar 2026) says the 2025 US-Japan agreement projected up to $100bn for Westinghouse reactors but specific projects were not yet identified and Westinghouse is still working transactions.

Second batch announced 19 Mar 2026 at the Takaichi-Trump summit lists SMRs by GE Vernova Hitachi in Tennessee and Alabama at up to $40bn; TVA Clinch River and Bellefonte/Widows Creek siting is from secondary reports.
Commerce lists gas generation in Pennsylvania at up to $17bn with offtake including co-located data centres; NextEra/South Mon 4.3 GW identification is secondary only.
Commerce lists gas generation in Texas at up to $16bn with offtake including data centres (second batch total about $73bn).

JBIC signed a loan of about $630m to Japan Invest 3 LLC on 17 Apr 2026 (total co-financing about $1.885bn) for a gas generation project integrated with data centre and transmission; NEXI insures private lenders; lenders unnamed.

Corporate relationships in the recommended compacts
Hitachi Energy pledged more than $1B for US grid equipment manufacturing including the $457M South Boston plant.

Nikkei reported in November 2025 that US Steel would build GOES capability at Big River Osceola Arkansas with mass production in 2028; US Steel confirmed the project to Argus without investment or capacity details (date approximate).
Toyota began production at its Liberty NC battery plant on 2025-11-12 (reported investment $13.9B with a further $10B pledged); output is mainly hybrid batteries and sources differ on line counts.
LGES agreed to sell the Ohio JV factory building and related assets to Honda for about $2.85B with the JV continuing via lease and closing targeted for 2026-02-28.

Panasonic plans to repurpose some US lines including De Soto to data-center energy storage with first cells expected mid-to-late 2028 or early 2029 while EV cell output continues; ramp is slower than planned.

Hitachi Energy broke ground on 2026-06-29 on a $457M South Boston expansion creating about 825 jobs; the site already employs about 850 and completion date was not stated on the page (other reports say 2028).
Unverified items are left out of this section; they stay in the evidence register (evidence_register.csv) and the evidence layer.

The relationship already has two working channels: an investment vehicle with a project pipeline and JBIC/NEXI finance (so far gas power, crude export, synthetic diamonds and SMRs), and a critical-minerals framework with financing, pricing and stockpile commitments but no published project list. What it lacks is a link between the two and any sector strategy for the electro-industrial chains where the data show complementarity.

Where the findings are weak or counterintuitive
Joint bets resting on a node need inherited from its cell (a proxy): Rare-earth oxides & compounds; Natural graphite; Polysilicon; Wind turbine generating sets.
Evidence-led compacts (OSI cannot see the partner's capability in trade data): Nuclear Fuel & Reactor Systems; Grid Equipment & Conductors.

Japan has no listed trade position (under 1% of world supply) at nodes where the US has material demand: solar cells, pv modules & generators, uranium/fuel extraction: aggregated low-coverage sub-sectors (spent fuel & nuclear scrap, uranium ores), uranium conversion & enrichment, nuclear reactors & enrichment machinery, lithium chemicals, pv cover glass, wind towers, heat pumps & ac units, solar thermal water heaters, electricity meters, transformers, hydro turbine parts, blade core wood (balsa), overhead conductors, aluminium wire rod, direct-reduced iron (dri/hbi). Trade data miss capability that is owned abroad or sold at home, so these nodes cannot show complementarity even where corporate evidence suggests it.

OSI reads transformers as low strategic case, but the evidence layer records a capacity problem the annual trade data cannot see: Wood Mackenzie projected a 30% supply deficit for power transformers and 10% for distribution units in 2025 with imports about 80% of power transformer supply and Q2 2025 lead times of 128 weeks (GSUs 144 weeks). Treat it as an emerging bottleneck to re-test, not a settled open-market node.

OSI reads grain-oriented-electrical-steel-goes as low strategic case, but the evidence layer records a capacity problem the annual trade data cannot see: Cleveland-Cliffs states Butler Works is the only US producer of regular grain-oriented electrical steel used in power and distribution transformers. Treat it as an emerging bottleneck to re-test, not a settled open-market node.
Low-evidence units among the active states: none.

Fuel-trade lanes reach tier 1 on Japanese import need (oil extraction): real energy-security lanes, but outside the electro-industrial compacts and with no market failure beyond the supply concentration the engine measures.
